newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky sees no need for referendum on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky sees no need for referendum on EMU.

text.p: Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said on Sunday he saw no need to hold a referendum in Austria on joining a European single currency but stressed that the advantages of membership had to be explained better to the people.
"At the present point in time, I see no need to hold a referendum on the Euro (European single currency)," he told Austrian television in an interview.

The chancellor, who has led the government for the past 10 years, said taking part in a common European currency had already been accepted by the Austrian people when two-thirds of voters backed EU membership in a referendum in June 1994.

Government and financial leaders are confident that Austria will meet by January 1999 the criteria outlined in the Maastricht Treaty for entry into the European economic and monetary union (EMU) and a single currency.

But far-right leader Joerg Haider's Freedom Party won nearly 28 percent of the vote in a European Parliament election last month, after basing his campaign mainly on lambasting Maastricht. He says giving up the stable schilling, which is pegged to the German mark, would be folly.
Vranitzky's pro-Europe policies have the firm backing of his Social Democratic Party and his coalition junior partner, the conservative People's Party of Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.
Vranitzky said the introduction of a single currency would "in the end have advantages for all EU members".

But the chancellor emphasised that it was vital to equip all the people, from schoolchildren to pensioners, with all the details on EMU and to outline all the disadvantages they would face if Austria stayed out of closer economic integration.

The government in March introduced a tough austerity budget for 1996 and 1997 to prepare Austria for EMU, but Vranitzky repeated that he did not believe it necessary to have another austerity budget in 1998.
Negotiations for the 1998 budget package would begin early next year, he added.
Vranitzky said Austria's neutrality was no hindrance to closer involvement in European security, and ruled out the holding of a referendum on whether to ditch the country's neutral status.

The chancellor, who was taken aback by the dismal performance of his own party in the Euro-election, said the government and the Social Democrats had to begin to go on the offensive to outline its ideas for the future.

The Social Democrats took just 29.1 percent of the vote in the European poll, an all-time low. Political analysts said around 50 percent of blue-collar voters, the Social Democrats' traditional supporters, backed the far right on fears over Europe and an influx of foreigners.
